item.title: D-Street’s stellar rally faces valuation test as bond allure grows
item.description: India's stock market is experiencing valuation challenges due to increasing bond yields that diminish equity attractiveness. The gap between government bond yields and stock earnings yield has widened significantly recently. Analysts suggest that high bond yields could hamper valuations as earnings struggle to catch up. Many global firms maintain a bullish outlook on India's market despite this pressure.
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: India’s stock rebound is approaching a crucial valuation test as rising bond yields make sovereign debt an increasingly viable alternative to equities.The gap between India’s benchmark 10-year government bond yields and the Nifty 50’s forward earnings yield has widened to about 1.95 percentage points, nearing the 2-percentage-point threshold that has proved difficult to sustain historically.Earnings yield — the inverse of the price-to-earnings ratio — measures expected earnings as a percentage of a stock’s price. A widening gap with bond yields means sovereign debt is offering greater returns at lower risk compared to equities, dimming the appeal of the Indian stock market.“This is my favorite valuation benchmark, which is a good rule of thumb to follow,” said Vikash Kumar Jain, Head of India Research at CLSA. “At the current level of bond yields, there is limited room for further P/E rerating until earnings catch up.”India’s 10-year sovereign bond yield is around 7.27%, compared with 5.3% for the Nifty 50’s 12-month forward earnings yield. The gap has widened from 1.24 percentage points at the end of September, when it was the narrowest in 19 months, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.136010782India’s sovereign bond yields have jumped this year, driven by a surge in crude prices, higher US Treasury yields and the Reserve Bank of India’s tighter monetary policy. Benchmark 10-year yields, which have risen around 70 basis points so far in 2026, approached a four-year high last month.At the current level of bond yields, Nifty would struggle to sustain a valuation above roughly 19-times, Jain said.At its October low, the multiple had fallen to 16.4x, the cheapest in more than six years and below its five-year average of about 19.3x. After the 15% rebound since Oct. 8, the Nifty 50 currently trades at about 18.8x estimated 12-month earnings.Read more: Reliance Industries share rebound is not over yet, says JPMorgan. Target price set at Rs 1,675“Valuations at current levels look full. In fact, we are factoring in a moderation of 2-3% in the forward P/E ratio over the next 12 months,” says Sunil Koul, global emerging-markets equity strategist at Goldman Sachs Group Inc.This comes at a time when many Wall Street firms have turned more bullish on India, drawn by its relative haven appeal as tech-heavy Asian markets gyrate with swings in the global artificial intelligence trade.Goldman Sachs expects the Nifty to reach 28,500 by end-2027, implying around 12% upside from Thursday’s close, while that of Citigroup Inc. is at 28,000. Both expect earnings growth — rather than increasing valuations — to do the heavy lifting.While Koul sees higher yields as a headwind, he doesn’t expect them to derail India’s broader equity story. The large weighting of banks in benchmark indexes could provide some insulation, as lenders stand to benefit from higher rates, he said.Read more: Trifecta effect! How RIL, HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank are powering Nifty rebound after 2 yearsElevated bond yields also pressure equity valuations by raising the discount rate applied to future corporate earnings.With the valuation cushion created during last month’s lows largely disappearing and bonds offering stiffer competition, further equity gains could hinge on stronger earnings or lower yields.“The easy part of the catch-up trade is now done,” said Jain. Indian stocks will need more catalysts to build on the rally, he said.
